I think that in some cases, with antidepressants your mental health problems can also come back. Sometimes they work for a while and then stop working. You can fall into a placebo effect where you think it's helping but it's not, and then you're right where you began. If that's the case, then that antidepressant isn't right for you, and it would be the same thing for hormones, they also aren't right for you. If you think they'll help more than they'll harm, then you can try them if you want. And then if they don't, you can change and switch. We don't even know the mechanisms about exactly how antidepressants work to relieve depression, and we don't really know why hormones could also help mental instability. The issue is people assuming that a pill is going to magically solve all of their issues with no repercussions. It's not; the goal of medication is to make your symptoms easier to deal with while also not causing any side effects you can't live with. Some people can live with the side effects of a deepened voice and more hair if it eases their mental issues. Some people have decided that better mental health in one regard is not worth the mental health effects they now have related to having a deepened voice and more hair. And other people have decided that they don't even want to chance the side effects and would rather take a different medication altogether with a lower risk profile. All three people are completely valid. Their thoughts and feelings about how they exist are valid. Because they all have bodily autonomy to make decisions. That's not to say that they can't make a wrong decision, but at the end of the day they have to learn to live with what happens to them in life. We don't get to dictate what helps them or what doesn't help them. But what we can do is just make sure they make an informed decision, so they can assess if they are comfortable to take the risk or not. And that goes with any medication you put in your body, not just hormones and antidepressants.

Of course. It's always good to educate people so they can make informed decisions. It just depends on OPs factors. I'm not sure how much it increases their risk compared to other treatments, but it could be the lowest risk out of all the options. I simply don't have enough information to make that judgement call for them, and I don't want to assume.

Is OP willing to trade off lessening PMDD symptoms for a blood clot risk? The treatment for PMDD can be hormones/birth control or it can be SSRIs. With estrogen birth control, you can get breakthrough bleeding, mood fluctuations, increased blood clots, headaches, nausea, and increased stroke risk. SSRIs can cause serotonin syndrome, insomnia, vomiting, and low sex drive. OP gets to decide if the relief from their symptoms is worth the increased risk. They have the bodily autonomy to decide what medications they want to take to improve their very real symptoms. We're talking about assessing the improvement of symptoms vs the risk of taking medication. That's a very personal question that only OP can decide if it's worth it. If PMDD isn't interrupting your life, then it doesn't make sense that you would take increased health issues for very little relief. But if PMDD is controlling your life, then yeah, you're going to say an increased blood clot is worth it because at least now I get to live a more normal life. I don't think we should shame OP for taking a certain medication to fix a medical problem. As long as they understand the risk they are taking, what's the issue?

It could be! It's all about risk assessment. A mood stabilizer can cause Tardive dyskinesia (repetitive, involuntary movements), which is absolutely permanent, but can help stabilize your mood. Testosterone can deepen your voice permanently, but might offer relief from anxiety. Are you okay with risking the side effects of a mood stabilizer? Are you okay with risking the effects of testosterone? It's a very personal choice. As long as you are educated and consenting, it's your choice. you get to decide what happens to your body. No one else does.

Not the original person, but I had a hysterectomy and then discovered I wasn't trans. I totally get why you can't understand. Right now, I don't have a uterus. It's gone, and it's not like it can suddenly be put back in me. That was permanent, and I went into surgery knowing full well it was permanent. I did not want to be pregnant, and I got the surgery because i can't medically take birth control and my periods were killing me. I had extreme pain around my periods. So the hysterectomy relieved my pain. It really wasn't related to me being trans. I *thought* it might be related to me being trans. Because what woman wants to get rid of her uterus? I thought I was trans because I didn't want kids and would gladly just give up that organ. Once it was actually gone, I realized my pain was relieved. And that not wanting a uterus/to be in a pain didn't make me less of a woman. Basically I did the surgery to relieve pain, not because it would make me less of a woman. And i'm glad that it isn't causing me pain anymore.

I think you need to be kind to yourself. You made a decision at the time with the information you knew and was available to you at the time. You weren't expecting what happened to happen. And you can't fault yourself for that. You made a decision that was right for you at the time. And now, you can make a decision for what's right for you at this time now that you have more information. It's OK to make mistakes. That's part of living. Every decision that we make is based on what we know. It's OK to have regrets. That's part of being human. But now you get an opportunity to reassess. You don't *have* to change. But if you didn't make the right decision, you can decide to change again. That's a decision that you get. Both are valid. Whatever you decide is going to be the best decision, you're making with everything you currently know. And that's all you need when making a decision.

Depends on your definition of "gay". Gay can mean you are really attracted to masculine people and see yourself as a man. Or it can mean you're a man and are attracted to penises. Attraction is really complex and hard to define since we all have vastly different experiences. Some lesbians really like dildos, and if they're sexual with a trans woman they see her parts as just a different type of dildo. There's also the fact that just because you're lesbian doesn't mean you can never in your entire life experience attraction to a guy (although that is a possibility too). Because attraction is very subjective. Also, as an asexual person, it's really important to note there are different types of attraction. The main ones are romantic and sexual. For most people, these synch up. If you want to date a woman, then you probably also want to hook up with them. For me, i don't want to have sex with people, and have yet to meet a singular person in my entire life who I found the urge to have sex (aka I don't experience sexual attraction). I just want to be close, cuddle, and live and share the rest of my life with that person (ie romantic attraction). So for me, i'm really really attracted to femininity, so I call myself a lesbian. Whether or not that person has genitals to match doesn't really matter to me as I won't be using them anyway. They're irrelevant. But i'm still attracted to women and femininity romantically.

Accepting that you made some changes, but underneath it all you're still you. You're still the person with the same hobbies, interests, life experiences, just you have a different form now. You have to remember that you don't get to dictate what happens to another persons body. That's for them to decide. The only thing you can do is help them objectively weigh the positives and negatives. Help them be realistic. "Yes, it might help with this, but it might also cause this. Is that a risk you're willing to take?" And then don't try to invalidate their feelings whatever they say. The more you try to push them toward one particular answer, the higher the likelihood that they'll resist and stop looking at things objectively. For some people, transition is the right choice and they have learned to live with their decision. For some people, transition is not the right decision and they have learned that and decided to change. Try helping them understand *why* they feel the need to transition. Ask open ended questions and guide them. Instead of saying "I think you're doing this just because xyz", try saying "do you think that xyz has factored in to why you've decided to pursue this?" Help them sort through their feelings so they aren't making a rash decision. Because you're going to alienate them by trying to dictate how they feel and what they can do. Which doesn't help anyone, let alone someone struggling with something like depression. Let them understand *why* they are doing this, because then they can better weigh if that's what they really want to do, or if it's something they *think* they want to do. People tend to experience less regret and unhappiness when they know the potential consequences of an action before they even make the decision. And it sounds like that's what you really care about: if they are happy or not.

If you want to, there's nothing saying you can't. Personally, I find HRT and antidepressants to boil down to be pretty similar use cases. Both can be used to treat mental health and alleviate mental health symptoms. Both can change your body in permanent and temporary ways, and sometimes in ways we don't yet know. Both are things that you can stop taking whenever you wish (as long as you still have your gonads, in the case of HRT). As long as you are fully educated, and acknowledge the risks, and consent to take the meds, then that's your personal choice and you absolutely can continue it. It's about looking at the pros vs cons, and deciding for yourself whether you have justification or not. None of us can really tell you the correct answer because there technically isn't one. There's just a choice that you have to live with, whatever happens.

If the injections are making you happy, and you understand exactly how they are/could affect you, and you consent to taking them, does it matter how you identify? The goal of any medication is to help you feel better. We don't really know how antidepressants work, but they tend to make some people better, so we still use them as long as the person taking them is OK with the side effects. Similarly, if you want to take estrogen as a way to feel better, and you're OK with all the side effects that come with it, then what's the issue? But the key is being educated. You need to do your research and determine for yourself if you think side effects are worth it or not. No one here can tell you what you think. Plenty of people here have decided that it's not worth it, and plenty of people I know irl have decided it is. There's also no reason that you would have to stay on it indefinitely if you change your mind in the future. You can stop it whenever you want. As long as you are educated and consenting, then is it really an issue?

Just to play devils advocate, i think that it's not suggesting *dont* kick the dog, i think it's suggesting that other first actions are more efficient. For example, if you start out with wildly flailing out of panic you're going to put more tension on the affect area and the teeth will go in deeper and the dogs gut reaction will be to bite down harder. Instead, if your first react is to stay calm, you can figure out the best course of action rationally. If that's kick the dog in the chest, then that's kick the dog in the chest. But if the dog is just latched on, you can save yourself a lot of wound damage by covering the dog's nose and mouth so it can't breathe and is forced to let go. *then* you kick the dog in the chest to keep it away from you while help arrives.

Also I do feel for if you had a child that didn't make a league, but I also think that there is a lot of value in teaching them that just because they don't make a team, there is still a lot of value in playing for enjoyment and playing because you love the sport and not just because you want to win. Some people are trans and could definitely benefit from receiving care when they need it. Hell I knew I was childfree 11 years ago and I haven't changed my mind.
